parts.note: a nap is the short sleep a drowsy person takes
kin are your family
a ring is a circle

explanation.surface: A sleepy family sits round in a circle aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is the old word for a dining table, so 'on board' is where the thing is found, not a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin ring holds a rolled serviette and sits at each place laid on the dining table.

wordplay.note: sane read as 'not insane': a two-word phrase, a negative followed by a word for crazy, run together

explanation.surface: A wandering tramp who is perfectly sound of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Sane means not mad, written here as the two words NO and MAD run together.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad wanders from place to place without a fixed home, as a vagrant does.

parts.note: surface reading: snappish dogs or bad-tempered people with a harsh voice
setter's reading: the bitter tree bark from South America that yields quinine, named after the country's people

explanation.walkthrough: Cinchona, the source of quinine, was long sold as 'Peruvian bark', so the people of that country own a bitter bark.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Peru gave their name to Peruvian bark, the bitter cinchona used against malaria.

parts.note: surface reading: dubious or suspect methods
setter's reading: procedures consisting of questions put to someone

explanation.definitionFit: Formal sessions of close questioning, as by police, are literally procedures made up of questions.

clue.text: That's one thing to do with the old

definitions.text: That's one thing to do with the old

parts.words: That's one thing to do with the old
parts.note: surface reading: a remark about caring for elderly people
setter's reading: Tennyson's line about New Year bells, telling them what to do with the old year

explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's In Memoriam has 'Ring out the old, ring in the new', a line quoted at every New Year.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells sound to dismiss the departing year, which is what the poem says to do with the old.

clue.text: Anniversary his fiancee asked Walter to

parts.note: surface reading: a bride-to-be asking her man to fix the wedding date
setter's reading: the yearly feast of the saint whose name a person bears

explanation.surface: A woman asks her fiance Walter to fix a date for something annual.
explanation.walkthrough: An engaged couple must 'name the day' for the wedding; split differently, the phrase is a yearly saint's feast.
explanation.definitionFit: A name day is the annual feast of one's patron saint, celebrated each year like a birthday.

clue.text: This programme was with it to a degree!

parts.note: taken as written
MA, Master of Arts, is a university degree

explanation.surface: A broadcast that was fashionable and up to date, to some extent.
explanation.walkthrough: ITMA, 'It's That Man Again', was a hugely popular BBC radio comedy of the 1940s.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC wartime comedy show was known everywhere by its initials, making it a radio programme.

indicators.note: something in a poor state is in bad shape, so the name's letters get knocked into a new order

parts.note: Oliver Twist, Dickens's orphan hero

explanation.surface: Someone jeers at the unfortunate orphan Oliver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor Oliver' reads naturally as pity for Dickens's orphan, but it marks a rearrangement of his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: To twit someone is to tease or mock them, so twits as a verb means teases or jeers.

parts.note: surface reading: the home of a collector of old things, or of Scott's novel The Antiquary
setter's reading: the seventeenth-century antiquary Elias Ashmole, whose collection is housed in an Oxford museum

explanation.walkthrough: Oxford's museum of art and archaeology was founded on the collection Elias Ashmole gave the university.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford museum named after antiquary Elias Ashmole is the building that houses his collection.

parts.note: surface reading: a place where physicians and members of parliament get together
setter's reading: doctors of law, gathered at the old London college where civil law was practised

explanation.walkthrough: Doctors' Commons was the London society of civil lawyers, abolished in the 1860s; MD stands for doctor and the Commons is where MPs sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic London college of doctors of civil law took its name from the doctors dining in common.

clue.text: In civil war an 11 place geographically

definitions.text: In civil war an 11 place geographically

parts.note: surface reading: a place of North African character in some civil war
setter's reading: a place followed by a Moor

explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is MOORISH, so 'an 11 place' is a place with a moor: Marston Moor, the 1644 Civil War battle near York.
explanation.definitionFit: Marston is a Yorkshire village beside the moor where Cromwell's forces won a major battle.

parts.note: surface reading: a North African follower of the Oxford Movement
setter's reading: relating to a tract of open land, like a heath, as well as meaning North African

explanation.walkthrough: Tractarians were Oxford Movement churchmen; here the word is split to mean 'of a tract' of upland heath.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both the Moors of North Africa and land that resembles a moor.

parts.note: surface reading: a route walked by Dickens's hero
setter's reading: the young hero walks from London to the Kent coast to find his aunt Betsey Trotwood

explanation.definitionFit: David Copperfield tramps the highway from London to Dover to reach his aunt, a famous chapter of the novel.

indicators.note: 'into' splits as 'in to', so the animal is placed inside the little word that follows

parts.note: taken as written
a donkey brays

explanation.surface: A braying donkey turns into a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' splits as 'in to': the donkey goes in the word to. Torquato Tasso was the Italian Renaissance poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso, author of Jerusalem Delivered, is a famous Italian epic poet.

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal word; the setter relies on the letters being plainly a shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall cylindrical military hat with a peak and plume.

parts.note: surface reading: the end of a road to riches
setter's reading: Flecker's poem The Golden Journey, whose pilgrims take the golden road to a Central Asian city

explanation.walkthrough: James Elroy Flecker's 1913 poem ends 'We take the Golden Road to Samarkand'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Silk Road city in Uzbekistan is the destination of the travellers in Flecker's famous poem.

clue.text: Early tea and cards will carry us over to Dundee

definitions.text: will carry us over to Dundee

parts.note: tay is how the drink was spoken in earlier centuries
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: Morning tea and a card game on the trip to a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: In Pope's day tea rhymed with obey; Dundee lies on the Firth of Tay in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The railway crossing over the Firth of Tay takes travellers from Fife into Dundee.

parts.note: surface reading: beds in an outer-town house, or the outskirts of Bedfordshire
setter's reading: a room full of beds, and a commuter suburb where people only sleep

explanation.walkthrough: A dormitory town or suburb is one whose residents work elsewhere and come home only to sleep; Beds is short for Bedfordshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: A dormitory is a sleeping room, and as an adjective describes a commuter suburb.

clue.text: Misled about California — got the name wrong me wrong

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps itself round the state's abbreviation

parts.note: taken as written
Cal. is an abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: Someone was steered wrong about California and mixed up a name.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a stray 'me wrong' at the end, apparently a typesetting slip.
explanation.definitionFit: To miscall something is to call it by an incorrect title.

parts.note: surface reading: an illness, and land planted with trees
setter's reading: Kipling's African river 'all set about with fever-trees'

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So story The Elephant's Child describes 'the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees'.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern African river is lined with fever trees in Kipling's famous description.

parts.note: surface reading: an infrequent guest at the poet's house
setter's reading: Shelley's poem 'Rarely, rarely, comest thou, Spirit of' a joyful feeling

explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's song opens 'Rarely, rarely, comest thou, Spirit of Delight!'
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the spirit of joy and pleasure seldom comes to the speaker, a rare visitor.

clue.text: Shepherd on his way to a Greek city

parts.note: surface reading: a shepherd travelling; setter's reading: the old shepherd in As You Like It

parts.words: on his way to a Greek city
parts.note: setter's reading: his name is the start of the name of the ancient isthmus city, short of its last two letters

explanation.surface: A herdsman is walking to a city in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: The shepherd's name is most of the way to Corinth: it lacks only the TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Corin is the old shepherd of the Forest of Arden in Shakespeare's As You Like It.

parts.note: surface reading: several people talked
setter's reading: the noun, a wheel rod running from hub to rim, in the plural

explanation.definitionFit: Spokes run from the centre of a wheel to its rim, so they lie along lines from the centre of a circle.

clue.text: Disastrous if their banks were liquidated

definitions.text: Disastrous if their banks were liquidated

parts.words: Disastrous if their banks were liquidated
parts.note: surface reading: a financial collapse when lenders are wound up
setter's reading: the dykes of a low-lying people turned to water, flooding the land

explanation.walkthrough: Much of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by dykes and embankments.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of the Netherlands rely on their banks and dykes to hold back the sea.

parts.note: surface reading: someone heard people singing
setter's reading: Jean Elliot's lament The Flowers of the Forest, which begins with lasses lilting at the ewe-milking

explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish lament opens 'I've heard them lilting at our ewe-milking'; the setter calls its author Jane.
explanation.definitionFit: The girls singing at the milking in Elliot's song are the farm's dairy maids.

parts.note: surface reading: an exclamation at a great catch
setter's reading: a cricket hit that goes high into the heavens, giving an easy catch

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a ball hit steeply upward is a catch waiting to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: A skyer is a cricket shot struck high into the air, usually offering a catch.

parts.note: surface reading: an unreliable seller of frozen desserts, presumably Italian
setter's reading: Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, a merchant who is an Italian

explanation.walkthrough: The title character of The Merchant of Venice shares his name with the stock Italian ice-cream seller.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is the Venetian merchant who pledges a pound of flesh to Shylock.

clue.text: Study that may lead to fault-finding

definitions.text: Study that may lead to fault-finding

parts.words: Study that may lead to fault-finding
parts.note: surface reading: a discipline that makes someone critical
setter's reading: locating fractures in rock strata

explanation.definitionFit: The science of rocks and the earth's crust involves identifying faults, the fractures in strata.

clue.text: Had turned fifty and brought a flower from Mexico

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the word before it is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone reached fifty and fetched a Mexican bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The dahlia, native to Mexico, is named after the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish botanist gave his name to the dahlia, a Mexican plant introduced to European gardens.

parts.note: sooth is an old word for truth
one who tells or says

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller, if the truth be told.
explanation.definitionFit: A soothsayer foretells the future, as a diviner or seer does.
